examples.title: Two classification lenses
examples.situation: Sort a tomato and a peanut for a market-use table, then identify their plant structures.
reasoning: A tomato develops from a flower and contains seeds, so it is a botanical fruit.
In the practical food-use table it is a fruiting vegetable; that does not undo its botany.
Peanut forms pods and belongs to the legume group, though its common name and oily seed may suggest a nut.
Peanut is not a FAO dry pulse; oilseed legumes are excluded from that narrower category.
examples.takeaway: Tomato: practical fruiting vegetable and botanical fruit. Peanut: legume, not a dry pulse. State which classification question is being asked.

examples.title: Four similar-looking harvests
examples.situation: A label says every upright vegetable is a stem and every underground swollen part is a root.
reasoning: Identify the actual harvested organ, not its position alone.
Celery's commonly eaten crisp stalk is a petiole; asparagus spears are young shoots/stems.
Potato forms a stem tuber, while sweet potato forms a storage root.
examples.takeaway: Revise the labels by organ. The two pairs demonstrate why visual position and culinary names are insufficient.

examples.title: What the bank analogy can and cannot tell us
examples.situation: A grower harvests maize grain, returns some stalks, then grows a legume and removes its harvested product.
reasoning: Harvest and removed residues export material; returned roots and residues may contribute to soil organic matter.
Legume nodules may fix nitrogen if the plant, rhizobia and conditions allow.
A numerical nitrogen credit needs crop history, harvest/residue details, soil assessment and a locally appropriate method.
examples.takeaway: Do not label the cereal an inevitable organic-matter loss or the legume an automatic full nitrogen refund.
